claim: A software company that deploys autonomous diagnostic tools in consumer-facing healthcare applications owes a non-delegable duty of care to end users who foreseeably rely on those tools for medical decision-making. The Ninth Circuit held that Nexalign's failure to implement adequate algorithmic safeguards constituted a breach of that duty, even absent a direct contractual relationship with the plaintiff.
citation: Everdeen v. Nexalign Technologies, Inc., 887 F.3d 412 (9th Cir. 2018)

claim: A retail chain's failure to inspect and remediate a known liquid spill near a high-traffic checkout area within a reasonable time constitutes a breach of the duty of care owed to business invitees. The Fifth Circuit held that constructive notice of a hazardous condition, established through surveillance footage showing the spill predating the injury by over forty minutes, was sufficient to sustain the plaintiff's negligence claim.
citation: Crenwelge v. Harborview Retail Partners, LLC, 883 F.3d 214 (5th Cir. 2018)
case_name: Crenwelge v. Harborview Retail Partners, LLC

claim: A pharmaceutical manufacturer owes a non-delegable duty of care to foreseeable end users when it knows, or reasonably should know, that inadequate labeling of a compounded drug creates a substantial risk of patient harm. The Third Circuit held that this duty arises independently of any contractual relationship between the manufacturer and the prescribing physician.
citation: Lourdeaux v. Meridian Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 743 F.2d 519 (3d Cir. 1991)

claim: A construction firm's failure to erect adequate barriers around an open excavation site constitutes a breach of the duty of care owed to foreseeable pedestrians in the surrounding area. The Third Circuit held that proximity alone is sufficient to establish the requisite duty relationship where the defendant's ongoing operations create an obvious and continuous hazard to the public.
citation: Xanthopoulos v. Delvecchio & Sons Construction, LLC, 837 F.2d 214 (3d Cir. 1991)
case_name: Xanthopoulos v. Delvecchio & Sons Construction, LLC

claim: A hospital system's duty of care extends to the timely communication of critical diagnostic findings to treating physicians, and failure to establish adequate internal protocols for such communication constitutes actionable negligence when patient harm results. The Ninth Circuit held that institutional negligence need not require proof of a single identifiable actor where systemic breakdowns in care coordination are demonstrable.
citation: Moltrasio v. Cascadia Regional Health System, 738 F.3d 201 (9th Cir. 2013)
case_name: Moltrasio v. Cascadia Regional Health System

claim: A pharmaceutical manufacturer owes a continuing duty of care to monitor post-market adverse event reports and warn prescribing physicians of newly identified risks, even where the drug received FDA approval at the time of initial distribution. Failure to update labeling upon discovery of such risks constitutes a breach of the manufacturer's duty of care under negligence doctrine.
citation: Ulbrecht v. Meridian Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 837 F.2d 514 (3d Cir. 1989)

claim: A county sheriff's department owes a cognizable duty of care to third parties foreseeably endangered by the negligent supervision of deputy personnel operating department vehicles during non-emergency patrols. The court held that institutional awareness of prior reckless driving incidents by a deputy created an affirmative obligation to intervene before harm materialized.
citation: Gruvenmacher v. Pellitier County Sheriff's Office, 318 F.3d 774 (4th Cir. 2001)
case_name: Gruvenmacher v. Pellitier County Sheriff's Office

claim: A software manufacturer owes a cognizable duty of care to end users when it has actual knowledge that foreseeable system failures in safety-critical applications could cause physical harm. The Ninth Circuit held that Meridian Dynamics could not disclaim liability through boilerplate licensing language where the risk of bodily injury was both known and preventable through reasonable design measures.
citation: Vanthorpe v. Meridian Dynamics Corp., 738 F.2d 419 (9th Cir. 1984)

claim: A financial institution owes a duty of care to elderly account holders when its employees have actual knowledge that a third party is systematically withdrawing funds in a manner consistent with exploitation. Failure to intervene or notify the account holder under such circumstances may expose the institution to liability in negligence.
citation: Holvenstot v. Meridian Bank & Trust, 874 F.2d 319 (7th Cir. 1991)

claim: A construction firm owes an affirmative duty of care to adjacent property owners when excavation activities foreseeably destabilize neighboring foundations, even absent a direct contractual relationship. The Fourth Circuit held that geographic proximity and knowledge of structural risk are sufficient to establish the duty element in a negligence claim against a commercial contractor.
citation: Ives v. Drakewood Construction Partners, 839 F.2d 214 (4th Cir. 1988)

claim: A state university owes a duty of care to visiting prospective students participating in campus-sponsored tour programs, and failure to maintain reasonably safe pedestrian pathways during foreseeable inclement weather conditions constitutes actionable negligence. The Fourth Circuit held that the university's awareness of recurring ice accumulation near the science quad, combined with its failure to deploy remedial measures, satisfied the breach element under a heightened invitee standard.
citation: Fenquist v. Appalachian State University, 883 F.3d 441 (4th Cir. 2018)

claim: An insurer owes an independent duty of care to its policyholders that extends beyond the contractual terms of the policy, requiring reasonable investigation before denying claims that could foreseeably cause substantial harm. The Fifth Circuit held that Meridian Coastal's failure to conduct any meaningful inquiry prior to denial constituted actionable negligence under Louisiana tort law.
citation: Velthorpe v. Meridian Coastal Insurance Co., 338 F.3d 712 (5th Cir. 2003)
case_name: Velthorpe v. Meridian Coastal Insurance Co.

claim: A pharmaceutical manufacturer owes an ongoing duty of care to monitor post-market adverse event data and issue updated warnings when emerging evidence reveals risks not disclosed at the time of initial approval. Failure to act on such data within a reasonable timeframe constitutes a breach of that duty sufficient to survive summary judgment.
citation: Crenwelge v. Vantara Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 891 F.2d 344 (5th Cir. 2019)

claim: A county sheriff's office owes a cognizable duty of care to detainees when deputies are made aware of a credible medical emergency and fail to act within a reasonable timeframe. The Fourth Circuit held that deliberate indifference to known physical distress constitutes a breach of that duty sufficient to sustain a negligence claim under § 1983.
citation: Rhovantis v. Caldwell County Sheriff, 748 F.3d 301 (4th Cir. 2019)

claim: A retail chain owes an affirmative duty of care to inspect and remediate known hazardous conditions in customer-accessible areas, and failure to act within a reasonable time after constructive notice constitutes actionable negligence. The Seventh Circuit held that Meridian Mart's internal maintenance logs demonstrating awareness of a recurring wet-floor condition were sufficient to establish that duty had attached prior to the plaintiff's injury.
citation: Ovelund v. Meridian Mart Holdings, Inc., 78 F.3d 441 (7th Cir. 1996)
case_name: Ovelund v. Meridian Mart Holdings, Inc.

claim: A municipality owes a cognizable duty of care to residents when it has actual notice of a dangerous condition on public property and fails to remediate within a reasonable time. The Sixth Circuit held that the Delphi City Council's eighteen-month inaction following written complaints about a collapsed drainage culvert was sufficient to sustain a negligence claim under Indiana tort law.
citation: Wrenshaw v. Delphi City Council, 238 F.3d 514 (6th Cir. 2001)

claim: A financial institution owes a cognizable duty of care to non-customer third parties when its employees' affirmative misrepresentations foreseeably induce detrimental reliance that results in quantifiable economic harm. The Fourth Circuit held that Pembrook Bank & Trust could not escape negligence liability by invoking the economic loss rule where the plaintiff's damages arose directly from a loan officer's unauthorized oral assurances rather than from any contractual expectation.
citation: Kelvridge v. Pembrook Bank & Trust, 238 F.3d 501 (4th Cir. 2001)

claim: A state university assumes an affirmative duty of care toward graduate research assistants when it exercises direct supervisory control over laboratory conditions, and failure to remedy known structural hazards in university-operated facilities may constitute actionable negligence. The Ninth Circuit held that institutional knowledge of a recurring danger, combined with inaction, satisfies the breach element under a heightened custodial duty standard.
citation: Wolthuizen v. Cascadia State University, 673 F.2d 441 (9th Cir. 1988)

claim: A retail chain's failure to inspect and remediate known wet flooring conditions near store entrances during inclement weather constitutes a breach of the duty of care owed to business invitees. The Seventh Circuit held that constructive notice of a recurring hazard is sufficient to establish negligence liability absent corrective action.
citation: Poltavsky v. Hargrove Retail Group, Inc., 778 F.2d 334 (7th Cir. 1988)
case_name: Poltavsky v. Hargrove Retail Group, Inc.

claim: An insurer owes a cognizable duty of care to its policyholders that extends beyond contractual obligations, requiring affirmative steps to investigate and communicate known risks that may foreseeably cause harm to the insured. Failure to discharge that duty, where the insurer possessed superior knowledge of the risk, constitutes actionable negligence independent of any bad-faith claim.
citation: Etzwiler v. Meridian Coastal Insurance Group, 778 F.3d 341 (4th Cir. 2019)
case_name: Etzwiler v. Meridian Coastal Insurance Group

claim: A municipal body assumes an affirmative duty of care when it undertakes infrastructure inspections and then fails to act on documented hazards brought to its attention by residents. The Meridian City Council's inaction following written notice of a collapsed storm drain was held sufficient to establish negligence liability under the foreseeable harm standard.
citation: Xanthopoulos v. Meridian City Council, 847 F.2d 391 (5th Cir. 1991)

claim: A pharmaceutical manufacturer owes a continuing duty of care to monitor post-market adverse event data and update warning labels accordingly, even absent new regulatory guidance. The Third Circuit held that Veridian's failure to act on internal safety signals constituted a breach of that duty sufficient to sustain a negligence claim.
citation: Xanthopoulos v. Veridian Pharma Solutions, Inc., 738 F.3d 512 (3d Cir. 2013)
case_name: Xanthopoulos v. Veridian Pharma Solutions, Inc.

claim: A state university's failure to adequately maintain and inspect pedestrian walkways on campus grounds gives rise to a cognizable negligence claim where the institution had actual or constructive notice of the hazardous condition. The Fourth Circuit held that the university's duty of care extended to all foreseeable users of university property, including visiting prospective students.
citation: Moutsatsos v. Hargrove State University, 589 F.3d 214 (4th Cir. 2009)
